subtype: Stage 4: First payment and sunk cost [Response]
passage: The hostel common room was empty except for the warden's radio when Disha's phone lit up again: "Final processing fee for your internship letter, Rs 4,000. Pay in 1 hour or your seat goes." She had already paid the Rs 1,500 "registration fee" that morning. Her thumb hovered over the payment app. Then she stopped. Every message had asked for one more thing. She took screenshots of the whole chat, the job letter and the payment receipt, and walked straight to the warden's office. Bhavna Ma'am read the screen, didn't say a word about being careless, and dialled the number on the back of Disha's bank card with her. The bank blocked further transfers and told her to report it on the cybercrime portal the same night. "The fifteen hundred may be gone," Bhavna Ma'am said. "Not sending the four thousand matters more." Disha nodded, shaky but lighter.

qa.q: How much had Disha already paid that morning?
qa.a: She had already paid the Rs 1,500 registration fee that morning.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she walked to the warden's office?
qa.a: She was frightened and embarrassed about the money already lost, but determined to stop before sending more.

qa.q: Which choices worked well here, and why?
qa.a: Disha stopped, saved screenshots and went to a trusted adult, and they called the bank on the card's own number, which blocked further losses the same day.

qa.q: How might Bhavna Ma'am see her role in this moment?
qa.a: Bhavna Ma'am likely sees that a calm, blame-free response helps Disha act fast, so she focuses on the next step instead of the mistake.

grounding: Shows someone who has already paid a scammer stopping, saving the messages and going to a bank and a trusted adult instead of chasing the loss.

passage:
"Mr Anirban? This is Inspector Rao, cyber cell. A parcel in your name has illegal items. There is an arrest warrant."
"What? I haven't sent any parcel."
"Then cooperate. Stay on this video call. Do not disconnect, or we treat it as absconding."
"Can I call my family first?"
"No. If you tell anyone, they become part of the case. Understand?"
The door opened. Vikas, his flatmate, came in with groceries. "Bro, did you eat?"
Anirban waved him away without looking up.
"Who is that? Are you speaking to someone?" the voice snapped.
"No, sir. No one."
"Good. We need to verify your accounts within twenty minutes, or officers will come to your office."
Vikas stood in the doorway. "Anirban? You're sweating."
Anirban turned his back to him and whispered, "Sir, what do I need to do?"

qa.q: Who came in with groceries?
qa.a: Vikas, his flatmate, came in with groceries.

qa.q: Why does Anirban wave Vikas away?
qa.a: He is terrified of arrest and has been told that anyone he tells becomes part of the case, so fear makes him hide the call.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Anirban at this moment?
qa.a: He could hang up, let Vikas see the screen, and check with the police through an official number, since real officers do not demand secrecy or keep people on video calls.

qa.q: What is it like for Vikas in the doorway?
qa.a: Vikas is confused and worried, seeing his flatmate sweating and whispering to someone yet being shut out.

grounding: Shows a victim told to act now, stay on the line and tell no one under a threat of arrest, with pressure and isolation shutting down careful thinking.

subtype: Stage 4: First payment and sunk cost [Receiver]
passage:
Note by Darshan, shift supervisor, packing unit, Thursday
Pranav came to me at lunch looking grey. On Monday he paid Rs 500 to "release" a parcel held at customs. On Tuesday they said the parcel needed insurance, so he paid 3,000. Today they asked for 12,000, a refundable clearance, and he had already started the transfer.
I asked why he kept going. He said, "If I stop now, the first two payments are wasted. And I'd have to tell my wife I was fooled." He kept saying he was not stupid.
What I did next: I told him plainly that the money already sent was probably lost, and that sending more would not bring it back. He cancelled the transfer in front of me. We called his bank on the number on the passbook, and I stayed while he filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal. I have given him the afternoon off to talk to his wife.

qa.q: How much did Pranav pay on Tuesday?
qa.a: On Tuesday he paid 3,000 for the parcel's insurance.

qa.q: What feelings kept pushing Pranav to pay more?
qa.a: He felt trapped and ashamed, afraid that stopping would waste the first two payments and that he would have to admit to his wife he was fooled.

qa.q: What turning point did the supervisor create, and why did it help?
qa.a: The supervisor said the money already sent was probably lost, which freed Pranav to cancel the transfer and report it the same day instead of chasing the loss.

qa.q: How might Pranav's wife be affected when he tells her?
qa.a: She may feel shocked and worried about the money, but hearing it that afternoon means they can face it together instead of him hiding more payments.

grounding: Shows a victim paying more after a small first transfer, trapped by the wish to recover losses and avoid admitting a mistake.

passage: In the bank's staff canteen, Payal pushed her dal around and kept checking her phone. The man she had been messaging for four months, a doctor working abroad, he said, had asked again for money to clear his "stuck" salary. Last week his camera was broken. Yesterday he wrote that he was in London; today the time on his message said it was 3 am there, yet he was "just finishing lunch." Payal noticed. She told herself time zones were confusing. Her colleague Sudha sat down. "You've been quiet all week. Everything okay at home?" Payal smiled too quickly. "All fine. Just tired." She could not imagine saying it aloud: that she, who processed loans all day, might have been fooled. Her mother would never let it go. Her cousins would hear by evening. She turned the phone face down and hoped, very hard, that she was wrong.

qa.q: Where did the man say he was yesterday?
qa.a: Yesterday he wrote that he was in London.

qa.q: Why does Payal smile too quickly when Sudha asks if everything is okay?
qa.a: Payal is afraid and ashamed, hoping the doubts are wrong because telling anyone would mean facing her mother, her cousins and her own sense of being fooled.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Payal right now?
qa.a: Payal could take up Sudha's opening and tell her what she has noticed, then check the man's story and send nothing more until she has spoken to someone she trusts.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel after Payal says all fine?
qa.a: Sudha may feel uneasy and unconvinced, having noticed a week of quiet, and may wonder how to ask again without pushing.

grounding: Shows a victim noticing inconsistencies but hoping they are wrong, with fear of shame and family reaction keeping her silent.

passage: I'm Gurpreet. I'll say what I saw in our flat in Shillong over those two weeks, though I can't know everything Lalremsiami felt. My wife started taking her phone into the bathroom. She'd leave dinner half eaten when it buzzed. Twice I saw her at the bank's ATM on a weekday afternoon, which she never does. When I asked, she said, "Just helping a friend." One night she was awake at two, typing fast, her face lit blue. I wanted to grab the phone. Instead I made two cups of tea and sat beside her. "You don't have to tell me everything. But whoever this is, can we call the bank together, on the number on your card, before you send anything else?" She was silent for a long time. Then she put the phone between us on the table, face up.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet see Lalremsiami twice on a weekday afternoon?
qa.a: Twice Gurpreet saw her at the bank's ATM on a weekday afternoon.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling at two in the night, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt worried and alarmed, wanting to grab the phone, but chose calm by making tea and sitting beside her.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's approach likely to work?
qa.a: Gurpreet asked calmly, without blame, did not demand the whole story and suggested one clear step: a pause to call the bank on the official number.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami be experiencing when she puts the phone face up?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and ashamed at once, finally letting someone in after two weeks of secrecy and rushed transfers.

grounding: Shows a family member noticing secrecy, rushed transfers and constant phone use, then calmly suggesting a pause to verify through an official channel.

passage: "Come, Lavanya, sit. You asked why I made you save the bank's number in your phone. Let me tell you about your cousin Nithya, last year, when she was twenty-four. A man called her saying he was from the bank. Her card would be blocked, he said, unless she shared the code that came by message. He was very polite, very urgent. She had already read out four digits when she stopped. Something in her said, why is the bank asking me? She cut the call. Then she did the clever thing: she opened the bank's own app and called the number printed there. They told her no one had called. She rang me next, crying, and I said, 'Report it now, don't wait.' So she called the bank to freeze the card and filed a report with the cybercrime helpline that same hour. Nothing was lost. That is why, kanna. Your Rukmini Paati is not just being fussy."

qa.q: How many digits had Nithya read out before she stopped?
qa.a: She had already read out four digits when she stopped.

qa.q: What was Nithya feeling when she rang Rukmini Paati?
qa.a: Nithya was shaken and frightened, crying after the near-miss, but also relieved that she had stopped in time.

qa.q: Which choice in the story was the turning point, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Nithya cutting the call and checking through the bank's own app and number broke the caller's urgency, and reporting it that same hour meant nothing was lost.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Paati have felt when Nithya called her crying?
qa.a: Rukmini Paati was probably frightened for Nithya but steady enough to tell her to report it at once, which is why she still tells the story.

grounding: Shows a victim stopping mid-scam, hanging up, checking through the official app and number, telling a trusted person and reporting quickly to the bank and cybercrime helpline.

passage: I'm Shreya, and I'll tell you how Yamini was after the scam, as far as I could see. For a week she wouldn't come to our Sunday lunches. When she finally did, she kept saying, "How could I be so stupid? I'm an accountant." She stabbed at her food as if it had done something to her. Our friend Rohit started, "Honestly, those investment apps are obvious-" and I kicked him under the table. I said, "Yamini, someone committed a crime against you. That's what happened. It's their fault, not yours." She looked at me for a long time. A month later she asked if she could speak at our building's residents' meeting. She stood up, hands shaking a little, and showed everyone the fake app and the messages. Afterwards, an old uncle from the fourth floor came up and said the same people had messaged him yesterday.

qa.q: Who came up to Yamini after the residents' meeting?
qa.a: An old uncle from the fourth floor came up and said the same people had messaged him yesterday.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel in the week after the scam?
qa.a: Yamini felt foolish and angry at herself, repeating how could I be so stupid and stabbing at her food.

qa.q: What response helped Yamini recover, and why?
qa.a: Calling it a crime against her instead of stupidity took the shame off Yamini, which later gave her the courage to share the story.

qa.q: How might the old uncle from the fourth floor see Yamini's talk?
qa.a: He probably feels grateful and protected, because her story helped him recognise the same pattern before he lost anything.

grounding: Shows a scam victim feeling foolish and angry, friends treating it as a crime rather than stupidity, and the victim sharing the story so others can spot it.

passage:
Monday: Aparna carried the drawing she had made for Charu's birthday all morning in her bag, a cat with a crown. She kept touching it through the zip.
Wednesday: at lunch, Charu gave out small blue cards to six girls in the class. Aparna waited with her hand half open. The last card went to the girl behind her. Aparna looked hard at her tiffin and ate every grain of rice, very slowly.
Friday: at home she didn't want to watch cartoons. When Amma asked what was wrong, she said, "My tummy hurts," and then, "Nothing." At bedtime she took the cat drawing out of her bag, folded it very small, and pushed it under her pillow.

qa.q: How many girls got blue cards from Charu?
qa.a: Charu gave small blue cards to six girls in the class.

qa.q: How can you tell Aparna felt hurt even though she said nothing?
qa.a: She stared at her tiffin and ate very slowly, then said her tummy hurt, which suggests a sharp, lonely ache she has no words for.

qa.q: How could Amma support Aparna at this stage?
qa.a: Amma could sit with Aparna, say it sounds like something sad happened, and gently ask about school without pushing, so Aparna can find words for being left out.

qa.q: How might Charu see the birthday cards?
qa.a: Charu may simply have had only a few cards to give and not noticed who was waiting, with no idea how much it hurt Aparna.

grounding: Shows a child left out of a birthday invitation feeling a big, personal hurt she cannot put into words.

passage: The school library was Lalit's favourite hiding place now. At break, Pallavi found him in the back row with a book he wasn't reading. "We're all going for the inter-house match after school. Coming?" Lalit didn't look up. "I've got stuff." It was the third time this month. Since the class trip, when nobody had saved him a seat on the bus, he had stopped messaging the group first. If they wanted him, they could ask. When they did ask, like now, he said no anyway, before they could change their minds. "You used to love these matches," Pallavi said. Lalit shrugged. "I like being alone. It's easier." Pallavi stood there a moment longer, then left. Lalit watched her go through the glass door, and something in his chest dropped. He turned a page, though he hadn't read it.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi find Lalit at break?
qa.a: She found him in the back row of the school library with a book he wasn't reading.

qa.q: Why does Lalit say no before the others can change their minds?
qa.a: Lalit is afraid of being rejected again after the bus trip, so refusing first feels safer even though it leaves him lonely.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Lalit or Pallavi here?
qa.a: Lalit could say yes once, even for a short while; Pallavi could keep inviting him and tell him plainly that she wants him there.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel walking away from the library?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel confused and a little hurt, wondering if Lalit is annoyed with her, since he used to love these matches.

grounding: Shows a teenager who stops reaching out, turns down invitations and says he likes being alone, protecting himself but losing the chance to connect.

passage:
Note from the drama club teacher, Tuesday rehearsal
Trisha has been with the club since August and is usually quiet but prepared. Today, during the scene break, Hemant laughed at something on his phone just as Trisha finished her lines. She went red, stepped back and did not speak again for the rest of the rehearsal. When the group chat went silent for an hour after she posted the new costume list, she messaged me: "I think everyone finds me annoying." In the next scene her voice was so low the others kept asking her to repeat, which made her more flustered.
What I did next: I checked with Hemant privately; he had been laughing at a video from his cousin and hadn't noticed Trisha at all. After rehearsal I sat with Trisha for a few minutes and asked what other explanations there might be for the laugh and the quiet chat. I have also paired her with Hemant for Thursday's prop work.

qa.q: What did Trisha post before the group chat went silent for an hour?
qa.a: She posted the new costume list.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling after Hemant laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and afraid, taking the laugh as a sign that everyone found her annoying.

qa.q: What turning point did the teacher offer, and why is it useful?
qa.a: The teacher helped Trisha look for other explanations for the laugh and the quiet chat, and paired her with Hemant so she can test her fear against real contact.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel if he learns Trisha thought he was laughing at her?
qa.a: Hemant would probably be surprised and a little sorry, since he was only watching his cousin's video and hadn't noticed her.

grounding: Shows a lonely teenager reading a laugh and a quiet chat as dislike, becoming more guarded and awkward in a way that feeds the fear.
